ton.label: -ton
ton.meaning: farmstead, estate, later village (Old English tun). Some -ston names are stan, stone

town.label: -town
town.meaning: town, farm or settlement (later English town, from Old English tun)

ham.label: -ham
ham.meaning: homestead, village (Old English ham); some are hamm, land in a river bend, which the spelling cannot separate

ing.label: -ing / -ings
ing.meaning: the people of, or place of (Old English -ingas, -ing)

ley.label: -ley / -leigh
ley.meaning: woodland clearing, later meadow (Old English leah)

bury.label: -bury / -borough
bury.meaning: fortified place, later manor or town (Old English burh); some -borough names are beorg, hill

field.label: -field
field.meaning: open land, cleared country (Old English feld)

ford.label: -ford
ford.meaning: ford, a river crossing (Old English ford)

den.label: -den / -dean
den.meaning: valley (denu) or woodland pasture for pigs (denn), Old English
top_share_areas: The City of Brighton and Hove

stow.label: -stow
stow.meaning: place, often a holy place or meeting place (Old English stow)

minster.label: -minster
minster.meaning: monastery or major church (Old English mynster)

wick.label: -wick / -wich
wick.meaning: specialised farm (often a dairy farm) or trading place (Old English wic, from Latin vicus)

chester.label: -chester / -caster
chester.meaning: Old English ceaster, a Roman fort or town (from Latin castra)

strat.label: strat- / stret-
strat.meaning: Old English straet, a paved road, often Roman (from Latin strata)

eccles.label: eccles-
eccles.meaning: church, from Brittonic, from Latin ecclesia

thorpe.label: -thorpe
thorpe.meaning: outlying farm (Old Norse thorp; a few are Old English throp)

toft.label: -toft
toft.meaning: site of a house, homestead (Old Norse topt)

holme.label: -holme / -holm
holme.meaning: island, dry ground in marsh, water meadow (Old Norse holmr)

kirk.label: kirk-
kirk.meaning: church (Old Norse kirkja). Counted in England only, because Scots kirk is an everyday word

betws.label: betws
betws.meaning: chapel, prayer house (Welsh betws, from Old English bedhus)

pit.label: pit-
pit.meaning: a portion of land, farm (Pictish pett)

bal.label: bally- / bal-
bal.meaning: baile: farm, homestead, settlement. In Irish names Bally- can also be beal atha, ford mouth

kil.label: kil- / kill-
kil.meaning: cill: church. Kil- can also be coill, wood, and other words

dun.label: dun- / dum-
dun.meaning: dun: fort, stronghold. Irish Don- is often domhnach, church

bel.label: bel- / bella-
bel.meaning: beal: mouth, approach (often to a ford)

by.Barnaby Green: may be the personal name Barnaby
